extracted.intended_audience: librarians, printers, book-designers, binders, publishers, and bibliophiles
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for designing, printing, and binding books so they are beautiful, durable, and fit for their contents; aimed at the production and conservation of well-made volumes. Covers materials, typography, layout, illustration, and library/storage considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness to content
rubrics_metrics.description: The book's physical form must be adapted to the literature it contains; the book should be an interpretation of its contents and an offering of homage to its worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mismatches (e.g., a tiny 'Little Classic' Josephus or a folio Keats). The setting must be appropriate to the literary dignity or character of the work; a beautiful outside with commonplace inside is a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and material quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A book should be legible, strong, and durable; publisher has responsibility to use good, durable paper, clear and durable ink, and sound materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheapening paper, ink, or binding shortens life and betrays the obligation to transmit records to the future. Consumers should insist on durability to control quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page proportions (width:height)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation of page width to height should normally fall between about 60% and 75% (width as percent of height); extremes (near 50% or much above 75%) offend beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A width near one-half the height is too narrow; much over three-quarters looks too square. The 'printer's oblong' (~58%) is the limit of stately slenderness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thickness proportion (book thickness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thickness must be in proportion to height and width; very chunky or squat volumes lack elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer expansion of a book's dimensions in height/width rather than thickness, since thickness increases demand on shelf space and reduces perceived grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner vs outer margin proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner margin should be half (or a little more than half) the width of the outer margin so that, when opened, the paired pages form three columns of equal width.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement balances the double diagram of two facing pages and avoids an overly wide inner column when the book is open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top vs bottom margin relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The upper margin of a printed page should be narrower than the lower; top margin should not exceed half the bottom margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page should read as a pair with its mate — top/bottom relation follows from inner/outer margin choices and diagonal alignment of type on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-page and diagonal alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Type and paper pages should as a rule be set on a common diagonal from the inner upper corner to the outer lower corner so top and bottom margins relate properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This diagonal alignment helps ensure harmonious proportions between top/bottom and inner/outer margins and contributes greatly to the design charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type selection and classical norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters must be beautiful individually and in combination; standard roman types (e.g., Caslon, Bodoni) are handsome norms for prose; Cloister Oldstyle is a safe norm for poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departures from these norms risk aesthetic failure unless the type is exceptionally fine; black-letter capitals are poor in combination and generally unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve ascenders/descenders and letter proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The body and limbs of lower-case letters (ascenders and descenders) must not be atrophied or distorted by type design or machine constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compressed modern types that shorten g, p, q etc. diminish typographic beauty; proper letter proportions contribute to beauty even if most readers don't consciously notice them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type size proportion and legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Type size must be proportioned to the page and column: not too large (wastes space) and not too small (strains the eyes and discourages reading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance rapid reading needs, storage economy, and readability; the wrong size harms both utility and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leading and line separation
rubrics_metrics.description: When type bodies are compressed, leading (line separation) may be required; leading must be proportioned so the color of the text block is even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too much leading creates an excess of white (dazzling/offensive); if leaded spacing is used it should be balanced with type size so the page's 'color' is harmonious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification and even text color
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification should be done individually for each line (not by fixed mechanical scale) so as to avoid streamlets/rivers of white; the visual 'color' of the type block must be even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even spacing, true registration and careful setting are necessary to prevent distracting patterns across the page ('zebra of black and white stripes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and typographic consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading must be trained and consistent and stand for more than mere correction of errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good proofreading ensures consistent typographic standards (spacing, hyphenation, initials, headings) that contribute materially to the beauty and readability of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presswork quality and registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Presswork must be strong and even; registration must be accurate so lines on facing pages show accurately back-to-back when held to the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak presswork or poor registration degrades legibility and the aesthetic unity of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of columns for wide pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide pages should be printed in columns to facilitate rapid reading and visual comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columns prevent excessively long line length that tires the eye and aid readability while preserving esthetic proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing, headlines, and typographic aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the eye every possible help: paragraphs, headlines, variation of type — insofar as these devices conform with the esthetic rights of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices should be used to aid reading without violating the overall harmony of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and line endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dividing too many words between lines; excessive hyphenation makes line endings bristle and harms beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful setting to minimize hyphenation and sensible hyphenation rules preserve page beauty and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of paragraphs and page breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: A paragraph should not end at the bottom of a page nor begin too near it; final pages should not be too empty nor completely full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicious pagination and content distribution across pages prevents awkward or jarring page endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title-page and minor parts' treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor parts — half-title, dedication, table of contents, preface, index — present opportunities to make or mar the whole; the title-page is especially important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these elements requires solution appropriate to the book's character; poor handling here undermines the book's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and placement of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations must be fit and not merely beautiful in themselves; strong black-line engravings suit books best; many pictures can make an esthetic mess of text and image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using white-line engravings or halftones, print them apart from the text or separate them with an opaque sheet; place captions facing plates so the reader need not turn pages to view legend and image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color usage and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Color (initials, rubrication, etc.) is a question of propriety; a beautiful black-and-white page is often best and color should be used only if certain and judicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decoration must serve literary and artistic fitness; improvement by color must be justified by the result and not the means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper color, texture, and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer papers that are durable and softly toned (antique/cream) rather than dead white; paper should not be too thick for the book's size and must balance opacity with lightness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Softened whites (creamy yellow) are more pleasing; paper that is too thick impairs opening and flow of pages; antique papers can be both esthetically and practically desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ink color and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use black or possibly dark blue inks that are clear and durable; avoid sallow inks that are offensive to sight and smell and lack permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early printing inks that remain bright after centuries are the ideal; ink choice affects both legibility and long-term survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sewing, spine structure, and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Sewing determines flexibility; a well-sewn book opens easily with flowing curves; primitive (structural) stitching producing raised bands is preferable to methods that show saw-marks or impair opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inner fold saw-marks that indicate structural weakness; headbands in early books are structural, though modern ones are often merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headband and joint treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The hinge (joint) must harmonize strength and beauty; binders should shave leather under the joint to get thinness without sacrificing strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful shaving of leather for the joint reconciles conflicting demands (thickness for strength vs thinness for beauty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover material and binding workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers should be of honest boards and clad with cloth or leather that resists wear and contains no seeds of deterioration; the binder's work should leave the book solid, flexible, and unmutilated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full leather (not merely back-and-boards) is preferred for the book beautiful; cloth may be acceptable where durable and attractive; the covering should suit the book's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover ornamentation restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration on the cover must be unobtrusive; blind tooling, stamping, gilding, and inlaying are successive degrees of ornament and must be used sparingly and appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a little ornament can lessen beauty if poorly applied; the decorative treatment should respect the book's nature and avoid excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge treatment and trimming
rubrics_metrics.description: Margins must be set correctly so edges need not be trimmed; untrimmed edges testify to integrity; top edges may be shaved or gilded for dust protection, but full gilt is generally inappropriate except for devotional volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-trimming that reduces intended margins; goffering or pictorial edges are eccentric and often barbaric; apply gilding only where suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of shelf-space and librarian preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should avoid needlessly large or thick books; librarians prefer books no bigger physically than necessary (convenient height 7–9 inches) and oppose swelling volumes that multiply storage costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive thickness, wasteful margins, and oversized type increase shelving cost; design choices should account for library storage and long-term preservation needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and balance of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauty of the book depends on perfect balance among its parts; no single element must dominate, and the total effect should be considered before individual details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving the book beautiful requires harmonizing proportion, type, paper, binding and ornament so that the whole, not any part, is the primary experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producer and consumer responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers, printers, and binders share responsibility for quality but the consumer (and librarian) ultimately controls standards by what they accept and purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consumers tolerate adulteration (cheap materials, poor workmanship), faults return to them; insistence on durable, well-made books pressures producers to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial economy and psychological ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book is worth writing, the author should draft, condense for compact expression, and arrange material to be most easily taken into the mind — not merely logical order but psychological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good content organization reduces production problems and benefits the reader; these editorial responsibilities affect the value of the finished book and the librarian's experience.
